text:
**Keep the Joins: The Case for Teaching Cursive in Primary School**

Every few years, a headline announces that handwriting is finished. Keyboards have won, the argument goes, so children should not spend precious hours looping their ls and joining their ts. Finland moved its curriculum toward typing, and plenty of American states let cursive lapse before some of them brought it back. The idea is tempting because it sounds modern and efficient. But it rests on a mistake about what a primary school is for. Schools do not teach handwriting only so that adults can fill in forms. They teach it because the act of forming letters shapes how children learn to read, spell, think and compose. Joined-up handwriting, taught well and without nostalgia, remains one of the best tools a primary school has. It should stay.

**What we are actually arguing about**

First, a clarification. Nobody serious proposes abolishing handwriting. The debate is about the final step: whether children should be taught to join letters in a flowing script, or whether print letters, perhaps supplemented by keyboarding, are enough. So the question is narrower than it first seems. The case against joining says that print is clearer, that it is what adults often write anyway, and that the hours spent on cursive would be better used elsewhere. These are fair points, and I will answer them directly. But I think the case for joining is stronger, for four reasons: motor fluency, the link between hand and mind, equity, and the simple fact that most people do end up joining their letters.

**Fluency is the point**

Consider what a child does when they write a sentence by hand. They must decide what to say, hold it in working memory, spell each word, and control a pencil, all at once. For a seven-year-old, each of those tasks competes for the same limited attention. If forming letters takes conscious effort, there is less attention left for ideas. This is why handwriting fluency matters: it frees up thinking. A child whose hand moves easily can concentrate on content.

Joined writing supports that fluency in a way print often does not. When letters are printed, the pencil lifts after every letter. Each lift is a restart: a new decision about where to place the next stroke. In a joined script, the pencil travels through whole words, and the word becomes a single movement rather than a string of separate ones. Teachers who use well-designed joined styles often notice that spelling patterns become automatic partly because the hand learns them as units. Common endings such as -ing, -ed and -tion become familiar shapes the hand can reproduce without thought. I would not claim this is proven to be dramatically superior in every study, since the research is mixed and often small in scale. But the mechanism is plausible, and the practical experience of many teachers points the same way.

It also helps with a problem that print creates: reversals. Children writing b and d in print often confuse them, because the two letters are mirror images that start from different points. In most joined schemes, both letters begin with the same movement, an entry stroke that comes from the baseline. The letters stop being near-mirror images in the hand, even if they still look similar on the page. This is a modest benefit, but it matters for the children who struggle most.

**Hand and mind**

The strongest argument for handwriting in general, and one that carries over to the joined form, concerns what happens in the brain when children write by hand rather than type. Studies comparing the two, including work using brain imaging with children and adults, have found that handwriting letters engages the brain differently from pressing keys. A key press is the same movement for every letter, while a handwritten letter requires a distinct, shaped movement for each one. That difference seems to help children recognize letters and learn to read. There is also evidence that taking notes by hand pushes students to summarize rather than transcribe, which supports understanding. Again, the evidence is not unanimous, and some of the famous results have proved harder to replicate than first hoped. Honest advocates should say so. Still, the overall direction is consistent enough that a school should be cautious about abandoning a skill that may be doing more cognitive work than we realize.

Joined writing is the most developed form of that skill. It asks for more planning of movement, more rhythm and more control than print does. If the benefit of handwriting comes partly from the richness of the motor task, then the richer task is the better one to teach.

**Speed without sloppiness**

The most practical reason is also the most ordinary. Children need to write quickly and legibly, especially under exam conditions. Printing at length is slow and tiring. Children who print throughout school often reach secondary level and discover that they cannot keep up with the pace of note-taking or timed writing. What happens next is telling: they begin to join their letters anyway, but without instruction. They invent their own half-joined hybrid, often inconsistent and sometimes illegible. Many adults write this way. The result is not freedom but a lack of teaching. It is far better to give children a clear model early, when their motor habits are forming, than to leave them to improvise at fourteen.

This is where the objection about time bites hardest, so let me take it seriously. Teaching cursive does cost classroom minutes, and primary timetables are crowded. But the cost is smaller than critics suggest. Short, frequent practice, ten minutes a day, is more effective than long lessons, and handwriting practice can be woven into spelling and composition rather than treated as a separate subject. The real question is whether those minutes are well spent, and I think they are, because they build a skill that is used across every other subject for the rest of a child's schooling.

**Equity**

There is a fairness argument that I think gets too little attention. Children arrive at school with very different experiences of writing and of devices. Some have parents who read to them, buy them pens and sit beside them while they practise. Others do not. Handwriting is one of the few areas where a school can directly and cheaply teach a physical skill to everyone, regardless of what is available at home. It needs a pencil and paper, not a tablet, a licence or a charger.

Keyboards, by contrast, are not equalizers. Access to well-maintained devices varies hugely between schools and homes. A curriculum that leaned on typing in place of handwriting would quietly favour children who already have devices and a quiet place to practise. And typing itself needs teaching: touch typing takes real effort to master, and a child who hunts and pecks is no faster than one who writes. If we want to teach keyboard skills, we should, but alongside handwriting and not instead of it.

There is also a particular benefit for children with certain learning differences. Many teachers and specialists report that a consistent joined style helps children with dyslexia and dyspraxia, because the continuous movement reduces the number of decisions required and makes spelling patterns more tactile. Not every child benefits, and some find joining harder, which is why flexibility matters. But a school that teaches joining well can support these pupils better than one that does not teach it at all.

**The objections**

Three objections deserve a reply. The first is that print is clearer and that many adults print. True, but clarity is a matter of teaching, not of letterform. Clear cursive exists, and unclear print exists. The second objection is that cursive is a relic: no one needs it. But this overlooks that people still sign documents, write notes, fill in forms, leave messages and take notes in meetings, and that reading the handwriting of previous generations, from a grandparent's letters to historical archives, depends on being able to read joined script. A child who cannot read cursive is cut off from a great deal of the written past.

The third objection is that insisting on joining is rigid. Here the critic has a point, and my position should accommodate it. Schools should teach joining as a default, not as a doctrine. A child with a physical difficulty should be able to adapt. A child who, at secondary level, settles into a style that mixes print and joins should not be penalised if it is legible. The goal is a fluent, legible hand, not a perfect copy of a copybook. Teaching a model is not the same as demanding that everyone adopts it forever.

**Conclusion**

The case for keeping joined-up handwriting does not depend on sentiment. It depends on fluency, on what we know about how hand movement supports learning, on the plain practicalities of exams and note-taking, and on fairness for children who rely on school to teach them skills that others learn at home. The evidence is not conclusive on every point, and anyone who says otherwise is overstating it. But when a skill is cheap to teach, plausibly good for learning, useful for life and equitable in reach, the burden of proof falls on those who want to drop it.

Digital skills matter, and children should learn to type. But they do not have to choose. A good primary school can teach both, giving typing a place and keeping the pencil in hand. Joined-up writing should remain on the timetable, taught briefly, regularly and flexibly, because it gives children a fast, fluent and personal way to put their thoughts on the page.

(Approx. 1,500 words)
